rule_name: Headings must be question or search-style queries
description: All H2 and H3 headings must be phrased as questions or natural search-style queries that a user would actually type, not as statement/label-style headings.
check_logic: Extract all H2/H3 headings from the article. For each, evaluate whether it is phrased as a question (ends in '?' or uses interrogative structure like 'How', 'What', 'Why', 'Can', 'Should', 'Is') or a natural search-style query, versus a flat statement/label (e.g. 'Screen Time Management' is bad; 'How Can Parents Limit Screen Time?' is good). Flag any heading that reads as a topic label rather than a query a real user would type into a search engine.

rule_name: Every section must have a clear purpose
description: Every section under a heading must do at least one of: explain something important, answer a user question, or give practical/actionable guidance. Sections that do none of these should be flagged for removal or merging.
check_logic: For each H2/H3 section, evaluate the body text and classify it against three purposes: (1) explains a concept, (2) directly answers the heading's implied question, (3) gives practical/actionable guidance. Flag any section that does not clearly serve at least one of these — e.g. purely narrative/scene-setting sections with no explanatory or actionable content.

rule_name: FAQs must reflect real user search questions
description: FAQ questions must reflect what real users actually search for, not editorial, rhetorical, or internal/meta questions about the article itself.
check_logic: For each FAQ question, evaluate whether it plausibly matches a real search query pattern (e.g. matches 'People Also Ask' style phrasing) versus being an editorial/self-referential question (e.g. 'Why is this quote relevant to this article?' is bad; 'How can parents help kids avoid X?' is good). Flag any FAQ that reads as internal commentary rather than a genuine user question.

rule_name: FAQs must be simple and conversational
description: FAQ questions and answers must use simple, natural, conversational phrasing rather than stiff or overly formal language.
check_logic: Evaluate FAQ question and answer phrasing for conversational tone — contractions, plain vocabulary, direct sentence structure — versus stiff, jargon-heavy, or overly formal phrasing that a typical user would not naturally type or expect to read.

rule_name: Minimum FAQ count
description: Each article must include at least 5 FAQ questions.
check_logic: Count the number of distinct FAQ question entries in the article. Flag if count < 5.

rule_name: Competitor review FAQ must include direct brand comparison question
description: Competitor review articles must include an FAQ question in the exact pattern 'Is [Competitor] better than [Brand]?' with a structured, direct answer.
check_logic: For articles tagged as competitor_review_articles, search FAQ questions for a pattern matching 'Is {competitor_name} better than {brand_name}?' (or close semantic equivalent). Flag if no matching FAQ entry is found.

rule_name: Author must be named with a credential-based bio
description: Every article must have a named author whose bio states credentials, role, or relevant expertise — not a tagline or brand personality line.
check_logic: Check whether an author name is present. Then evaluate the bio text: does it contain a role/title and expertise statement (good, e.g. 'Digital safety researcher with 10 years in child psychology'), or is it a tagline/personality phrase with no credential content (bad, e.g. 'Dreams big, strategizes smarter' or 'Word-Alchemist who loves to bleed passion on paper')? Flag bios that contain no verifiable role, title, or expertise claim.

rule_name: Author bio must state name, role/title, and relevant expertise
description: The author bio must explicitly state the author's name, their role or title, and expertise relevant to the specific article topic.
check_logic: Parse the author bio for three components: (1) full name, (2) role/title, (3) an expertise or experience claim that is topically relevant to the article's subject matter. Flag if any of the three is missing, or if the expertise claim does not match the article's topic (e.g. a general 'parent and writer' bio on a clinical/medical topic).

rule_name: Author bio must include LinkedIn URL
description: The author block must include a link to the author's LinkedIn profile.
check_logic: Search the author bio block for a URL matching the pattern 'linkedin.com/in/*'. Flag if absent.

rule_name: Clinical topics require credentialed reviewer if writer is uncredentialed
description: For clinical or mental-health-adjacent topics (e.g. addiction, mental health), if the primary writer is not credentialed in that field, the article must include a 'Reviewed by [name], [title]' credit from someone who is.
check_logic: Classify the article topic as clinical/mental-health-adjacent or not. If clinical, check whether the author bio contains relevant clinical credentials (e.g. psychologist, therapist, MD). If the author is not credentialed, check for a separate 'Reviewed by' credit with clinical credentials. Flag if topic is clinical and neither the author nor a reviewer has relevant credentials.

rule_name: Technical topics require citation or credit to a technical authority
description: For technical topics (e.g. security exploits, bypass methods, software mechanics), the article must cite or credit a technical authority if the writer is not one.
check_logic: Classify the article topic as technical/security-adjacent or not. If technical, check whether the author has relevant technical credentials, or whether the article credits/cites a technical expert or authoritative technical source elsewhere in the content. Flag if neither is present.

rule_name: Author bio must not be a bare tagline
description: One-line brand-voice taglines with no credential content are not acceptable as an author bio and must be rewritten.
check_logic: Same core check as 'author-named-with-bio' — evaluate whether the bio is exclusively a stylistic/personality tagline containing zero factual credential, role, or expertise information. This is a duplicate/reinforcing check for the same underlying failure mode called out separately in the source document's checklist.

rule_name: Title must be under 60 characters
description: The post title (including spaces) must be under 60 characters to avoid truncation in search engine results pages.
check_logic: Count total characters (including spaces) in the post title field. Flag if length >= 60.

rule_name: Primary keyword must appear in title
description: The article's designated primary/focus keyword must appear in the post title.
check_logic: Given a designated primary keyword/keyphrase for the article, check whether it (or a very close variant/lemma) appears as a substring in the post title. Flag if not found.

rule_name: Title must not use decorative prefixes
description: Titles must not use decorative, non-keyword-bearing prefixes (e.g. seasonal taglines) that consume character space without adding search value.
check_logic: Evaluate the title's opening segment (before the first colon or clause break) for whether it carries keyword/search value or is purely stylistic/decorative (e.g. 'March Into Mindful Tech:' is decorative and should be flagged; a keyword-bearing lead-in is acceptable). Flag decorative prefixes, especially when combined with a title-length violation.

rule_name: Minimum external citation count
description: Each article must include at least 3 external citations to credible outside sources.
check_logic: Count distinct outbound hyperlinks to external (non-owned) domains that function as source citations for a factual claim. Flag if count < 3.

rule_name: At least one citation in first 40% of content
description: At least one external citation must appear within the first 40% of the article's total content length.
check_logic: Calculate the character/word offset marking 40% of total article body length. Check whether at least one external citation link falls before that offset. Flag if the first citation appears later than the 40% mark, or if no citations exist at all.

rule_name: Citations must be placed directly after the relevant claim
description: Each external citation must be placed immediately after the specific factual claim it supports, not batched elsewhere or disconnected from context.
check_logic: For each factual/statistical claim in the article, check whether a supporting citation link appears in the same sentence or the immediately following sentence. Flag claims that appear unsupported, or citations that are disconnected from any specific claim (e.g. dumped in a generic 'sources' list with no inline attribution).

rule_name: Citations must come from acceptable high-authority sources
description: External citations should come from academic/research papers, institutional reports (e.g. Pew Research, UNICEF, OECD, WHO), trusted scientific publications (e.g. Nature, Science, MIT), or official health/government bodies (e.g. AAP, NHS, CDC) — not low-authority or unverified sources.
check_logic: For each external citation, classify the linked domain/source type against an approved-source-tier list (academic journals, government/institutional bodies, recognized research organizations, established scientific publications). Flag citations pointing to low-authority sources (e.g. unrelated blogs, unverified forums, content farms, or the reviewed competitor's own unverified marketing claims presented as fact).

rule_name: Minimum internal link count
description: Each article must include 2 to 4 internal links to other previously published articles on the same site — not solely to the homepage or a pricing/product page.
check_logic: Count internal (same-domain) hyperlinks in the article body, excluding links to the homepage root URL and the primary pricing/product page. Flag if the count of qualifying internal blog-to-blog links is below 2 or above 4.

rule_name: At least one internal link in the middle of the article
description: At least one internal link must be placed in the middle portion of the article, not clustered only at the start or end.
check_logic: Calculate the character/word offsets marking the middle third of the article body. Check whether at least one qualifying internal link falls within that range. Flag if all internal links are clustered in the first or last third only.

rule_name: At least one internal link in a solution/action section
description: At least one internal link must appear within a section that gives practical guidance or actionable steps, not only in introductory or explanatory sections.
check_logic: Identify sections classified as action/solution/guidance-oriented (per the section-purpose-check logic). Verify at least one internal link falls within such a section. Flag if all internal links are located only in explanatory/background sections.

rule_name: Internal link anchor text must be descriptive
description: Anchor text for internal links must be descriptive of the linked content's topic, not generic phrases like 'click here' or 'read more'.
check_logic: For each internal link, extract the anchor text and check against a denylist of generic phrases (e.g. 'click here', 'read more', 'this article', 'here', 'learn more' when used as the sole anchor). Flag any match.

rule_name: Intro must define the topic in the first 2-3 sentences
description: The article's opening 2-3 sentences must clearly and directly define the core topic, rather than opening with scene-setting, narrative hooks, or background context.
check_logic: Extract the first 2-3 sentences of the article body. Evaluate whether they contain a direct, extractable definition or answer to 'what is [topic]' — versus narrative/atmospheric opening lines that delay the definition. Flag if a clear definition is not present within the first 2-3 sentences.

rule_name: Topic must not be re-defined later in the article
description: The core topic should be defined once in the intro; later sections should explain, expand, or exemplify — not restate the same definition.
check_logic: Compare the intro's definition sentence(s) against the opening sentences of each subsequent H2 section using semantic similarity. Flag any section whose opening closely re-states the intro's definition rather than building on it with new information (e.g. two near-identical 'X is defined as...' sentences appearing in both the intro and a later H2).

rule_name: Key Takeaways section must be present immediately after intro
description: A Key Takeaways section (a short bulleted summary) must appear directly after the introduction paragraph, before the first main body section.
check_logic: Check for a distinctly labeled block (heading or callout containing 'Key Takeaways' or close equivalent) positioned immediately after the intro paragraph and before the first H2. Flag if absent or if positioned elsewhere in the article.

rule_name: Key Takeaways must contain 3-5 bullets, no sub-bullets
description: The Key Takeaways section must contain exactly 3 to 5 top-level bullet points, with no nested sub-bullets and no paragraph-style content.
check_logic: Count the top-level list items within the Key Takeaways block. Flag if count is outside the 3-5 range, or if any nested list items (sub-bullets) or non-list paragraph text are present within the block.

rule_name: Key Takeaways must cover what/why/action
description: The Key Takeaways bullets must collectively cover: what the topic is, why it matters, and what the reader/parent can do about it.
check_logic: Classify each Key Takeaways bullet into one of three categories: definitional ('what it is'), significance ('why it matters'), or actionable ('what to do'). Flag if the bullet set does not include at least one bullet from each of the three categories.

rule_name: Key Takeaways should include one brand mention where natural
description: The Key Takeaways section should include one natural mention of the brand/product, where relevant to the topic.
check_logic: Check whether at least one Key Takeaways bullet references the brand name in a natural, non-forced way. Flag if the brand is entirely absent from this section, or if the mention feels inserted without topical relevance.

rule_name: At least one real-world example must be included
description: Each article must include at least one real-world example: an anonymized parent/user story, a behavior scenario, or a community insight.
check_logic: Scan the article for a distinct narrative example — identifiable by first-person or named-individual framing (e.g. 'Sarah, a mother of two, noticed...') distinct from generic instructional prose. Flag if no such example is present.

rule_name: Real-world examples must be visible text, not embedded in images
description: Real-world examples, testimonials, or quotes must appear as machine-readable visible text in the article body — content embedded only inside an image file does not satisfy this rule, since AI crawlers and search indexers cannot read image text.
check_logic: Verify that the identified real-world example content exists as plain HTML/text content, not solely as alt-text-less content inside an element. Flag if a testimonial or example appears to exist only within an image asset with no corresponding visible text block.

rule_name: Real-world examples must be properly sourced or clearly labeled as illustrative
description: If a real-world example includes specific, checkable details (exact numbers, named public incidents, identifiable biographical/medical specifics), it must either be properly cited to a real public source or explicitly labeled as an illustrative/composite scenario — not presented as a verified anonymized case study without either safeguard.
check_logic: Evaluate real-world examples for specificity level (exact statistics, unusual/checkable biographical details, named incidents). If specificity is high, check whether the example includes an external source citation. If no citation exists, check whether the text explicitly signals the example is illustrative/composite/anonymized-for-teaching-purposes. Flag high-specificity examples that are neither cited nor labeled as illustrative — this is a fabrication/misattribution risk.

rule_name: Minimum word count for standard articles
description: Standard articles must be at least 1,700-1,800 words.
check_logic: Calculate total word count of the article body. For articles classified as 'standard' (non-complex), flag if word count < 1700.

rule_name: Preferred word count for complex topics
description: Articles on complex topics should be 1,800-2,200 words.
check_logic: For articles classified as 'complex' (e.g. multi-faceted, research-heavy, or comparison-driven topics), flag if word count falls outside the 1800-2200 range.

rule_name: Minimum word count for competitor review articles
description: Competitor review articles should be 1,500-1,800 words minimum.
check_logic: For articles classified as competitor_review_articles, flag if word count < 1500.

rule_name: Article must include at least one clear brand CTA
description: The article must include at least one clear, explicit call-to-action directing the reader toward the brand's product (e.g. 'Try [Brand]', 'Learn more', 'Explore plans').
check_logic: Scan article body and any embedded CTA elements for text matching brand-defined CTA phrase patterns (configurable list, e.g. 'Try {brand}', 'Explore {brand} plans', 'Start your free trial'). Flag if zero matches are found — note that CTAs embedded only in images without accompanying visible text/link do not count.

rule_name: Brand feature links must be tied to a use case, not just linked generically
description: When linking to the brand's product features, the link must be contextually tied to the specific parenting problem or use case being discussed — not just a generic link to the homepage.
check_logic: For each brand product/feature link, check whether it is placed adjacent to a discussion of a specific problem/use case the feature addresses, versus being a bare/generic link with no surrounding contextual tie-in. Flag generic homepage-only links that lack contextual framing.

rule_name: Brand must be mentioned at least once in the article
description: The article must reference the brand/product by name at least once — articles with zero brand mentions provide no commercial value regardless of traffic performance.
check_logic: Search the full article body for at least one occurrence of the brand name (case-insensitive, allowing for common variants). Flag if zero occurrences are found.

rule_name: Competitor review must include a feature comparison table
description: Competitor review articles must include a structured, side-by-side feature comparison table comparing the competitor against the brand — not a prose-only comparison.
check_logic: For articles classified as competitor_review_articles, check for the presence of a <table> element (or structured markdown table) in the comparison section. Flag if the comparison is present only as prose paragraphs with no structured table.

rule_name: Comparison table must have minimum 8 feature rows
description: The competitor comparison table must contain at least 8 distinct feature comparison rows.
check_logic: Count the number of feature rows in the comparison table (excluding header row). Flag if count < 8.

rule_name: Comparison table should use visual indicators for scannability
description: The comparison table should use clear visual indicators (e.g. checkmark/warning/cross symbols) rather than long text descriptions in each cell, for quick visual scanning.
check_logic: Sample cell content in the comparison table. Flag if the majority of cells contain long-form text sentences rather than short symbols, ratings, or brief labels designed for quick scanning.

rule_name: Comparison table must cover required feature categories
description: The comparison table must cover a defined set of core feature categories relevant to the product vertical (e.g. for parental control software: content filtering, screen time, app blocking, location/geofencing, monitoring, platforms, price).
check_logic: Check the comparison table's row labels against a configurable required-category checklist for the product vertical. Flag any required category missing from the table.

rule_name: Comparison table must be in a dedicated comparison section
description: The comparison table must be placed within a dedicated 'X vs [Brand]' section, not scattered elsewhere in the article.
check_logic: Check that the comparison table is located within a section whose heading matches a 'vs' or comparison pattern (e.g. '{Competitor} vs {Brand}'). Flag if the table appears outside such a section.

rule_name: Competitor review must include an 'At a Glance' summary box
description: Competitor review articles must include a structured 'At a Glance' summary box immediately after the intro, using labeled key-value pairs rather than a plain bulleted list.
check_logic: Check for a distinctly labeled block (e.g. 'At a Glance') positioned immediately after the intro paragraph, formatted as key-value pairs (label: value) rather than free-form bullets. Flag if absent or misplaced.

rule_name: 'At a Glance' box must contain required fields
description: The 'At a Glance' box must include: Best for, Not ideal for, Price, Platforms, Ratings (App Store and Google Play scores, each linked to the live store listing), and a one-line reason to choose the brand instead.
check_logic: Check the 'At a Glance' block for the presence of each required field label: Best for, Not ideal for, Price, Platforms, Ratings (with linked App Store and Google Play scores), and a brand-alternative line. Flag any missing field. Additionally flag if Price or Ratings values use approximate markers (e.g. '~') without a linked source.

rule_name: App store ratings must be linked and not approximate
description: Any App Store or Google Play rating cited in a competitor review must link to the live store listing and must not use an approximate figure (e.g. '~4.6') without a linked source.
check_logic: For each numeric rating value found in the review (e.g. matching pattern like '4.6/5' or '~4.6'), check for an adjacent hyperlink to a recognized app store domain. Flag any rating that either lacks a link or is prefixed with an approximation symbol ('~', 'approx.', 'about') without a linked source.

rule_name: Review must open with a direct verdict, not scene-setting
description: The first sentence of a competitor review must state a direct verdict on the product being reviewed. The article must not open with scene-setting, background context, or general industry framing.
check_logic: Extract the first sentence of the article body. Evaluate whether it delivers a direct, extractable verdict/recommendation about the reviewed product (good, e.g. 'X is worth it for parents who need Y, but not for Z') versus general scene-setting or industry-context framing with no verdict (bad, e.g. 'In a digital world where kids are constantly exposed to...'). Flag if no clear verdict appears in the opening sentence.

rule_name: 'Is [Competitor] better than [Brand]?' FAQ answer must be structured and substantive
description: The FAQ answer to the direct brand-comparison question must be structured (covering what the competitor does better, what the brand does better, and who each is best suited for) and at least 3-4 sentences long. A one-line non-answer like 'it depends' is not acceptable.
check_logic: Locate the FAQ answer matching the 'Is {competitor} better than {brand}?' question pattern. Evaluate sentence count (flag if < 3) and check whether the answer covers three components: competitor strength, brand strength, and audience fit. Flag shallow or single-sentence non-answers.
